newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Thousands protest in tense Albanian town.
newsitem.headline: Thousands protest in tense Albanian town.

text.p: Tens of thousands of mourners poured through the Albanian port of Vlore on Tuesday in an explosion of outrage at the funeral of an anti-government demonstrator killed in clashes with police.

"The police killed him!" a crowd of at least 30,000 shrieked as it filed behind the open coffin of Artur Rustemi, a shopowner who died of a bullet wound suffered during pitched battles in the same streets 24 hours earlier.
The city remained quiet throughout the day with uniformed police out of sight.

But as night fell, more than 10,000 people massed again in Vlore's Independence Square, where protesters had staged five days of peaceful rallies last week before violence first erupted on Sunday evening.

"We have come to Vlore to establish a dialogue between the people and the government, to solve the economic crisis and later the political crisis," Neritan Ceka, leader of the centre-right Democratic Alliance, told the crowd.
Outside the port, on Albania's main north-south highway, 5,000 protesters were on a march launched in the city of Fier, 35 km (25 miles) to the north.
Several protesters threatened to advance on the police station, a flashpoint in battles between frenzied protesters and riot police which have left three people dead and about 150 injured.
In the capital Tirana, 150 km (90 miles) to the north, parliament called an evening debate on Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi's proposal to introduce emergency rule in Vlore to quell the unrest.
But it was uncertain deputies would agree to curb civil liberties. Even deputies linked to right-wing President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party have expressed reservations.

Meksi has played an increasingly prominent role as the crisis deepens. He says the protests are part of a plot by extreme leftists and have nothing to do with the grievances of investors who lost life savings in pyramid investment schemes.
Rustemi, 33, was one of three people to die in two days of clashes between police and protesters who blame Berisha for the failed investment funds.

The mid-morning cortege through the streets of the port was led by three men carrying black-and-red national flags at half mast. Also held aloft were two portraits of Rustemi, a Moslem father of two who had invested his savings in the schemes.
"Berisha is filling our cemeteries!" cried the mourners, clapping in unison. The crowd was swelled by thousands of residents persuaded to leave balconies overlooking the route and join in the march.
One of Rustemi's four brothers said outside the family home: "The police killed him when he was asking for his money."
As marchers moved towards the harbour and on to a cemetery, the local Democratic Party was engulfed in flames and gutted within minutes. It was not clear what had started the blaze.

Some opposition politicians accuse Berisha's party of using proceeds from the investment funds to finance their re-election campaign last year. Western observers have criticised the election as unfair.
The other victim of Monday's street battles, who died of heart failure, was buried later in the day. About 150 people were injured in two days of clashes in the port.

In Tirana, about 150 protesters staged a brief protest in central Skanderbeg Square, shouting "Vlore! Vlore!" before scattering to evade riot police. About 2,000 people gathered for a second straight day in the southern city of Gjirokaster.
Opposition attempts to stage rallies in the capital have been broken up for two successive weekends by riot police.

The opposition Forum for Democracy has urged residents instead to shut down schools and shops for two hours each day and called another rally for Wednesday. But the government has issued a fresh ban on the gathering
